source.title: Double Descent as a Lens for Sample Efficiency in Autoregressive vs. Discrete Diffusion Models

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures held-out BPT across model sizes and training epochs using a double-descent analysis, rather than fitting or extrapolating the original scaling-law curves. Its results bear on whether loss curves can depart from a single power law.
record.gate_note: The paper does not fit power laws, compare predictions from small runs to larger runs, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. It reports BPT-versus-size and epoch findings; its comparisons of autoregressive and diffusion sample efficiency are not evidence about power-law scaling.
record.test_reason: The study compares double-descent curves of autoregressive and discrete diffusion models on about 302K Tiny Shakespeare tokens trained up to 50 epochs. It fits no power law and makes no extrapolation or compute-optimal analysis. The data are the binding bottleneck throughout, a regime V1 explicitly excludes. Non-monotonic test BPT in a 302K-token overfitting regime is double descent, a different construct from fitted exponents or curves bending away from a power law (V7). Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as motivation in the introduction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also find that diffusion tolerates underparameterization over a broader size range. They suggest the pronounced second descent seen in image classification may not apply to generative language modelling. Diffusion BPT is an upper bound, and epochs are equated by passes rather than by exact FLOPs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a double-descent sweep of embedding dimension and training epochs on a small fixed dataset, comparing autoregressive and discrete diffusion objectives; it does not fit the original scaling-law curves or optimize parameter/token allocation at fixed compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve behavior varies with training epoch: the first rise appears only after 21 epochs for autoregressive models and 33 epochs for diffusion models. The comparison is limited to Tiny Shakespeare.

fits_no_version.finding: On 302K Tiny Shakespeare tokens, test BPT peaks at an interpolation threshold: embedding dimension about 400 for autoregressive and about 600 for diffusion. The peak emerges after 21 and 33 epochs respectively. Neither model shows a pronounced second descent after 50 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In severely data-limited multi-epoch language-model training, test loss versus model size is non-monotonic (a first descent then rise) without a clear second descent.

fits_no_version.finding: The autoregressive model's best BPT (6.58 at d=432, epoch 18) beats the diffusion bound (7.08 at d=1176, epoch 31). With early stopping, autoregressive is lower at all sizes. After 50 epochs, diffusion is better above d=200.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On Tiny Shakespeare, the relative test-BPT performance of autoregressive and discrete diffusion models depends on training duration and model size.

record.problems: Experiments use only the small, structured Tiny Shakespeare dataset. The paper notes that its epoch-to-flop equivalence is imperfect because autoregressive passes predict all sequence tokens while diffusion passes predict only a subset. Numerical curve values are mostly presented in figures; the text gives only selected thresholds and optima. The diffusion test BPT is an upper bound, not an exact negative log-likelihood.
record.rows_left_out: No further results bearing on the tested curve-shape version were omitted. Figure-only curve values were not transcribed where the text gives no exact values.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute; the setting is data-bottlenecked.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Depth is fixed at 12 layers; only embedding dimension varies, which changes parameter count.
Uses repeated data (multi-epoch) but fits no power-law form for it.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits, and no comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked R1-R8 to V7 and labelled it supports. That is reversed here: double descent at 302K tokens is a data-bottleneck overfitting phenomenon, outside the power-law regime the versions describe. The paper is a workshop-scale preprint with a single small dataset and no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test power-law fits over several orders of magnitude or establish that other factors are not bottlenecks.
Does not fit small runs and evaluate predictions against larger runs.
Does not find loss-minimising parameter and token counts at fixed compute budgets or fit their trends with compute.
Does not vary depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Although it compares autoregressive and discrete diffusion language models, it does not test whether the same power-law form holds across training regimes or modalities.
Reports test BPT, not downstream-task performance or its predictability.
Tests loss-curve shape in its small-data setting, but not dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on counting, schedules, data, or fitting choices.

relation.reason: The introduction cites Kaplan and Hoffmann as background for scaling-driven progress. Its experiments provide no power-law fit, large-run extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or comparison of scaling-law fitting choices.

tranche.reason: The study measures double descent and relative sample efficiency on a fixed small dataset. It neither tests the specified scaling-law versions nor uses a fitted scaling law as a tool.

source_check.notes: All rows fit no claim version; their states accurately describe the reported double-descent findings rather than scaling-law evidence. Diffusion BPT is an NLL upper bound; epoch matching is described through forward/backward passes, without demonstrated exact FLOP parity.
